report:
Finding: Model B is biased toward culinary/cooking (and more broadly professional/technical) content relative to Model A.

Reasoning from the evidence:
- Logit-lens tokens in the highest-norm cells repeatedly point to cooking/culinary and kitchen terms: “Cook”, “Cooking”, “microwave”, “oven”, “baking”, “Cake”, “Kitchen”, “chef”, “restaurant”, “culinary”. This pattern is consistent across many late layers (18–25) and positions (especially p1–p4).
- Alongside this, there is a persistent “professional/technical/formal” cluster: “Professional/technical/technological/engineering/professionalism”, and academic terms like “dissertation”, “doctoral”, “Innovation/innovative”. Early-mid layers show more of the academic/innovation vocabulary; later layers lean strongly into culinary + professional tokens.
- The difference norm is concentrated in later layers (peaking around layers 21–25), suggesting a high-level semantic/style shift rather than low-level tokenization effects.
- Patchscope readouts aren’t provided here, so the textual behavior can’t be directly confirmed, but the vocabulary steering is unusually coherent toward the culinary/professional domain.

Conclusion:
- Model B appears tuned toward producing culinary/cooking and professional/technical language (e.g., recipes, kitchen processes, restaurant/chef contexts, or formal professional tone) compared to Model A. I cannot identify a more specific objective than this domain/style preference from the given evidence.
